newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FROM THE HILL - The left's vows still some way off.
newsitem.headline: FROM THE HILL - The left's vows still some way off.

text.p: Labour and the Alliance seem to have come to terms with their opposing views on a political marriage -- the Alliance insists on a pre-nuptial agreement before the election and Labour prefers to wait for wedding night at the earliest.
But don't send out the invitations yet. There is still a chasm between them over protocol once the votes are counted.

This week Alliance leader Jim Anderton set out his conditions for a relationship. While their different approaches (if not differences) mean a marriage is out of the question, Anderton proposed a formula for a de facto arrangement.
That sees his party refuse point blank to support a minority National government, while offering to support Labour, New Zealand First or a combination of the two so long as:
a) there is an agreed programme (with the Alliance retaining the right to vote according to its manifesto on elements outside the programme) and,
b) an on-going process of consultation on legislation the government wants to bring into the House.

The agreed programme would not be a "sell-out" because it would be explained to Alliance supporters as the best the party could negotiate. Something like: "Not perfect, but better than the status quo or National".

Labour leader Helen Clark welcomed the Alliance's affirmation it would not support a conservative government and also gave the thumbs up to the Alliance, even outside government, having a legitimate role in negotiating policy if it supported a minority Labour government on confidence issues.
But that is where, to change the metaphor, the Mexican standoff resumes.
Clark was careful to order the "bridges" the Alliance would have to cross. First, it should agree to support Labour on confidence. Then it would be part of the negotiation process.

Anderton, on the other hand, is aware that once he has given support on confidence he is in Labour's embrace. So he wants a public statement of an agreed programme before granting his confidence. He would then make "a clear public statement" of the type the Governor-General has said he wants, and follow it up with a letter to Sir Michael Hardie Boys.
So Labour and the Alliance are back to their "before and after" rules. For Clark support comes before the chat. For the Alliance there is no blank cheque on confidence without an agreement.
Of course if the numbers fall the way of the left they will have to resolve this, and each has a view.

As far as Clark and deputy leader Michael Cullen are concerned, the Alliance could not risk not supporting Labour. The alternative would be National or a new election... and voters are traditionally harsh on minor parties.
From Anderton's side they say there is no way Labour would turn down a chance at government rather than reach for the phone and compromise.
Neither is the complete answer, but together they provide the imperative for each side to deal.
But no one can make a government until the chief electoral officer sings, and in the meantime some of the parties' main themes for the campaign are beginning to emerge.
For National read responsible stability.
For Labour read the responsible alternative with a heart.
For New Zealand First read New Zealanders First.
For the Alliance read leadership you can trust.
And the main targets are also apparent.
For National it is vote splitting towards its potential partners ACT and the Christian Coalition, as well as avoiding loss of provincial support to New Zealand First.
For Labour it is the "wet" National vote and supporters using their list vote to "experiment".
For New Zealand First it is to add National's rural-provincial heartland to its elderly-Maori vote (and to lessen the impression a deal with Labour is inevitable).
For the Alliance it is convincing the anti-government vote that a vote for New Zealand First is not a sure-fire vote against National.
Prepare to be bombarded.
-- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473-4746
